Nature Club / MAKE · LEARN · DISCOVER

Make a leaf rubbing.

Lay a leaf down. Rub. Watch the magic appear.

Ages 3–815 minOutdoors & indoors

Every leaf hides a pattern of veins and edges. With thick crayons and plain paper, children can lift that pattern into view, compare leaves side by side and turn their rubbings into creatures and big pictures. The five Leaf Studio pages below turn each step into a draw-and-save activity.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Gather your bits.

Tick things off as you get ready.

A note for grown-ups

Collect fallen leaves from the ground, or pick with permission, and brush off dirt and insects. Wash hands after handling leaves. An adult helps with scissors when cutting out rubbings, and nothing found outside goes in anyone's mouth.

A little more guidance ↗
ONE STEP AT A TIME

Let's make it happen.

  1. Go on a leaf hunt

    Collect five or six fallen leaves in different shapes and sizes. Brush or wipe them clean and let them dry flat.

  2. Set up your rubbing station

    Lay one leaf vein-side up on the table, cover it with a thin sheet of paper and hold it still.

  3. Make the rubbing appear

    Peel the paper off a thick crayon, lay it on its side and rub gently across the paper. The leaf appears like magic.

  4. Try pressures and colours

    Rub the same leaf lightly, then harder. Try two colours on one leaf and talk about which version you like best.

  5. Compare your leaves

    Make a rubbing of two different leaves on one sheet. Look closely: what is the same and what is different?

  6. Turn rubbings into art

    Cut out your favourite rubbings and arrange them into a leaf creature or one big picture. Glue, then add details.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

What's happening here?

A rubbing captures texture rather than shape alone: the veins, edges and bumps that make every leaf different. Noticing those details builds observation skills, and controlling crayon pressure builds steady hands.

Keep the wondering going.

  • Which leaf made the darkest rubbing?
  • What happens if you turn the leaf over before you rub?
  • Can you find a leaf with teeth on its edge?

Make it work for you.

Keep it simple

Choose big, strong leaves with deep veins, such as sycamore or maple. Place your hand over your child's hand and rub together, naming the leaf parts as they appear.

Take it further

Sort your rubbings into a classification chart by edge shape or vein pattern, then label each group. Try hatching two colours across one leaf and predict the blended result.

Not quite going to plan?

If the rubbing looks patchy, the leaf has probably slipped. Tape the leaf to the table under the paper, or hold it steady with two fingers while you rub.
